reasoning: 1. TARGET ENGAGEMENT: Strong evidence of target engagement. APL-130277 (sublingual apomorphine) is a dopamine D1/D2 receptor agonist. The MDS-UPDRS Part III motor score changes of up to -23.2 points at 30 minutes post-dose across multiple timepoints (Weeks 24, 36, 48) directly reflect dopaminergic receptor activation driving motor circuit improvement. This is a well-established pharmacodynamic readout for dopamine receptor agonism in Parkinson's disease. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: The downstream biology (dopaminergic motor circuit activation) clearly moved. The consistent MDS-UPDRS Part III improvements across all measured timepoints and weeks demonstrate that receptor agonism translated to motor circuit activation. The time-course data (peak effect at 30 minutes, declining at 60-90 minutes) is consistent with the pharmacokinetic profile of sublingual apomorphine. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: The clinical endpoints translated well. 80.7-87.3% of instances achieved full ON response within 30 minutes across weeks 24-48. The MDS-UPDRS Part III improvement of ~22-23 points at 30 minutes is clinically meaningful (a change of >10 points is generally considered clinically significant in PD). This is a single-arm open-label long-term safety study, so no comparator is available, but the effect sizes are large and consistent. 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: No subgroup analyses were reported. The enrolled population (PD patients with motor OFF episodes) is the appropriate target population for this mechanism. 5. CONFOUNDERS: This is a single-arm open-label long-term safety study (primary endpoint: number of participants with adverse events), so there is no placebo control. The primary endpoint was a safety endpoint (met: 365/496 participants had AEs over ~3 years, which is expected in a long-term safety study of an elderly PD population). The efficacy data (ON response rates, MDS-UPDRS changes) are secondary/exploratory but consistently positive. The cardiac SAEs (AMI, cardiac failure, cardiac arrest) are low incidence (<1% each) and likely reflect background cardiovascular risk in an elderly PD population rather than drug-related toxicity. No dose-limiting toxicity pattern is evident. The trial was designed as a long-term safety extension, and the primary endpoint (safety) was met in the sense that the safety profile was characterized. The efficacy signals are strong and consistent across the 3-year follow-up period.

failure_modes.evidence: Single-arm open-label design with no comparator limits causal inference for efficacy endpoints. Effect sizes are large and consistent, but without a control arm, placebo response contribution cannot be excluded. This is a design caveat rather than a true failure mode.
